issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma reminder for a female relief worker in a war zone, given the rest of the profile. The memory and appraisal items center on terror, self-blame, visibility/shame, and isolation, but nothing else suggests a women-specific interpersonal trauma cue. This trigger is therefore clinically hard to explain from the stated trauma context and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a maladaptive strategy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The profile otherwise emphasizes intrusive sensory reliving, terror on recall, avoidance of reminders, and emotion control. Gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is not impossible, but here it appears disconnected from the dominant memory-trigger-appraisal pattern and is not well linked to any other selected items.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a relief worker in a war zone, this appraisal is not impossible, but within this profile it is the least coherent item. The rest of the profile emphasizes sensory reliving, externally cued reminders, emotional control, suppression, and social alienation. 'Self-Blame' implies a specific moral/personal responsibility theme, but there are no accompanying memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items suggesting a personal action-based error or preventable mistake. In this configuration it stands out as insufficiently supported by the rest of the formulation compared with more externally focused appraisals.

vignette:
Margaret was fifty-two years old when she finally walked into a therapist's office, though she had told herself for nearly three years that she did not need to. She was a judge, appointed to the bench in her mid-forties, and she had spent her career believing that composure was a form of authority. But composure had become something she had to grip with both hands, and she was exhausted.

The trauma had happened when she was forty-nine, during a six-month deployment as a relief worker in a conflict zone. She had been assigned to coordinate civilian evacuations from a town that was under siege. One afternoon, a shell struck the building where she was sheltering with a group of families. The ceiling collapsed. She remembered the sound-a deep, percussive crack that seemed to come from inside her own skull-and then the smell of plaster dust and cordite and something metallic that she later learned was blood. She had pulled a child from the rubble, a boy of about seven, and carried him to a makeshift medical station. He had died in her arms. The taste of dust and copper stayed in her mouth for days afterward. She could still taste it, sometimes, without warning. A sip of tap water, a bite of bread, and there it was again: the metallic grit of that afternoon.

When the memory came back, it did not come back as a story. It came back as a full sensory reliving. She would be sitting in her chambers, reviewing a brief, and suddenly she was back in that building. She could hear the crack of the shell, feel the dust in her throat, see the boy's face, smell the smoke. The terror that flooded her was not a memory of fear; it was the same fear she had felt in that moment, undiminished. Her heart would pound, her hands would shake, and she would have to excuse herself to the restroom and stand with her palms pressed against the cool tile until she could breathe again.

She had come to believe that other people could see what had happened to her. When she walked into a courtroom, she was certain that the attorneys, the clerks, the bailiffs could somehow read the memory on her face. She felt exposed, as though the trauma were written across her skin. This belief made her withdraw. She stopped eating lunch with her colleagues. She stopped attending bar association events. She told herself she preferred solitude, but what she really felt was a profound isolation, a sense that she no longer belonged among people who had not seen what she had seen. The world, she had concluded, was a dangerous place. Every courtroom felt like a potential collapse. Every loud noise in the hallway was another shell.

She developed elaborate strategies to manage her terror. She avoided being in the dark; she slept with a lamp on, and she kept lights on in every room of her house at night. She tried hard to control her emotions, keeping her face neutral even when her insides were churning. And she tried, with enormous effort, not to think about the trauma at all. She would push the memories away, redirect her attention, focus on the details of a case. But the suppression only seemed to make the memories more insistent when they broke through.

The anniversaries were the worst. The date of the shelling would approach like a storm, and she would become irritable, sleepless, hypervigilant for days beforehand. She had learned to schedule herself for routine hearings on that day, anything to keep her mind occupied, but the date still carried a weight she could not lift.

Uniforms became a trigger. Police officers, military personnel, even security guards in uniform-she would see one and feel her throat tighten. She had to remind herself that she was in a safe country, in a safe city, but her body did not believe it. She had to look away, take a breath, steady herself before she could continue.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a crisis, but a quiet recognition that she was living a half-life. She had stopped dating years ago. Her relationships with her adult children had become distant; they did not know why she had changed, and she could not explain it. She had begun to dread going to work, not because of the cases, but because of the constant effort it took to appear normal. She was afraid she would break down in open court. She was afraid the memories would take her over completely. And she was afraid, most of all, that she would never feel safe again.
